Chart a series over time from a bundled dataset

Source: R/trend.R
btg_plot_trend.Rd

Draws how a measure moves across the years, or months, a dataset holds: a force's or council's stop-rate ratios or rates per 1,000 residents for each group compared with White, national monthly stops by group, national totals and rates by year, outcome-linked search rates by group, or a force's Section 60 searches by group. Each group keeps its colour from btg_group_colours() in every chart. Periods the source does not cover in full, or for which a force's returns were incomplete, are drawn with hollow markers and named in the subtitle; nothing is annualised.

Usage

btg_plot_trend(x, measure = NULL, highlight = NULL)

Arguments

x

A dataset from btg_get_data(). Force- and council-level datasets must be selected down to one area with the force or council argument of btg_get_data().

measure

What to draw. The default is the dataset's first measure: "ratio" or "rate" for the comparison datasets; "stops" or "share" for national monthly stops; any total or rate column of national_year; "hit_rate" or "hit_total" for outcome-linked search rates; "s60_stops" for Section 60 searches.

highlight

Optional name of one series (a group) to emphasise. The other series are drawn in grey as context.

Value

An editable ggplot with its evidence table, available through btg_figure_data() as one row per period and series with value, lower, upper, complete and months_in_source, and a saved view that btg_save_view() and btg_from_view() replay.

Details

Ratios carry their 95% Poisson intervals as vertical lines. Rates per 1,000 residents and counts for an incomplete period are lower simply because fewer months are covered; the ratio of two rates from the same months is unaffected by that, which is why incomplete periods are shown rather than dropped, but marked. Resident populations are fixed at Census 2021 for every year, so a trend in a rate reflects recorded stops only, not population change. A ratio is descriptive and does not establish discrimination.

Examples

met <- btg_get_data("force_ethnicity_year", force = "metropolitan")
btg_plot_trend(met)

btg_plot_trend(met, measure = "rate", highlight = "Black")

btg_plot_trend(btg_get_data("national_month_ethnicity"), measure = "share")

btg_plot_trend(btg_get_data("hit_rate_ethnicity_year"))
